title: Navigation Risk Management & Electronic Flight Bags

questions.text: During cruise flight, the autopilot begins an unexpected nose-up pitch. The airspeed is decreasing and the pilot doesn't understand why the aircraft is climbing. What should the pilot do FIRST?

options.label: A
options.text: Press the Autopilot Disconnect button and hand-fly the airplane. When the autopilot does something unexpected, unexplained, or uncommanded, the FIRST action is always to disconnect and take manual control. Stabilize the aircraft (lower the nose, verify airspeed, check attitude). THEN troubleshoot the autopilot to determine what mode caused the behavior. Never attempt to troubleshoot while the autopilot is still driving the aircraft into an unsafe state.

options.label: B
options.text: Check the Flight Mode Annunciator to determine which mode the autopilot is in. Understanding the mode is essential before taking any corrective action.

options.label: C
options.text: Push the yoke forward to counteract the nose-up pitch while the autopilot remains engaged. The pilot can manually override the servos to correct the pitch attitude.

options.label: D
options.text: Press the altitude hold button to change the autopilot mode. This will stop the climb and level the aircraft.

questions.explanation: The Disconnect Doctrine: DISCONNECT FIRST, troubleshoot later. Option B is logical but delays taking control — checking the FMA while the aircraft is pitching up and decelerating costs precious airspeed and altitude. Option C is dangerous — fighting the autopilot servos without disconnecting can create an extreme out-of-trim condition that produces a violent pitch excursion when the servos release. Option D attempts to fix the automation while it's misbehaving — the pilot may press the wrong button or enter a worse mode.

questions.text: During a VFR cross-country, the GPS suddenly displays 'RAIM NOT AVAILABLE' but continues to show the aircraft's position on the moving map with no other error indication. What should the pilot understand about the current GPS position?

options.label: A
options.text: The GPS is still computing a position, but it CANNOT verify the integrity of that position. Without RAIM, the receiver cannot detect if one of the satellites is transmitting corrupted data. The position shown on the moving map may be accurate — or it may be silently drifting from reality without any visual warning. The pilot should NOT trust the GPS as the sole navigation source. Cross-reference with VOR, pilotage, or dead reckoning until RAIM is restored.

options.label: B
options.text: RAIM is only needed for IFR precision approaches. For VFR en-route navigation, RAIM status has no practical effect on GPS accuracy.

options.label: C
options.text: The position is still fully accurate because the GPS has enough satellites for a 3D fix. RAIM is an optional enhancement that provides extra precision.

options.label: D
options.text: The GPS has failed and is displaying cached position data. The pilot should power-cycle the GPS to re-acquire the satellite constellation.

questions.explanation: RAIM is the GPS receiver's integrity monitoring system. Without RAIM (requires 5 satellites with good geometry), the receiver cannot cross-check the satellite signals to detect corruption. The position may be accurate or may be drifting — the pilot has no way to know. This is different from total signal loss (Option D) — the GPS is still computing, just without the ability to verify. Option B incorrectly limits RAIM's relevance to IFR. Option C misunderstands RAIM as precision enhancement — it's integrity verification.

questions.text: A Part 91 VFR pilot carries an iPad with ForeFlight as their sole navigation and chart reference — no paper charts, no backup device. Is this legal?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, it is legal. AC 91-78A explicitly authorizes Part 91 operators to use an EFB as a complete replacement for paper charts, provided the display shows functionally equivalent information and the database is current. The AC does not MANDATE a backup device for Part 91 operations. However, the AC heavily RECOMMENDS a backup as a fundamental best practice. While legal, flying with a single iPad and zero backup represents a significant risk management failure — one thermal shutdown or software crash leaves the pilot with no charts and no navigation.

options.label: B
options.text: No. AC 91-78A requires at least two independent navigation sources (primary and backup) for any flight, whether VFR or IFR.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, but only if the pilot has completed an FAA-approved EFB training course and carries the endorsement in their logbook.

options.label: D
options.text: No. EFBs are only authorized as supplements to required paper charts. Paper charts must be carried at all times.

questions.explanation: AC 91-78A is permissive: it authorizes EFBs as a complete replacement for paper charts. It does not mandate a backup for Part 91. However, it heavily recommends one. The legal answer is 'yes' — but the risk management answer is 'this is dangerous.' A single device with no backup is a single point of failure. Option B invents a dual-source requirement. Option C invents a training requirement. Option D is outdated — EFBs can fully replace paper.

questions.text: During a VFR cross-country, a pilot drops a pen. It rolls under the rudder pedals. The pilot leans forward and reaches under the panel to retrieve it. What is the primary danger of this action?

options.label: A
options.text: Cognitive tunneling — the pilot's entire attention shifts to retrieving the pen, causing the instrument scan and external visual scan to collapse completely. While the pilot is reaching under the panel, they are NOT monitoring heading, altitude, airspeed, or the horizon. In as little as 3-5 seconds of unmonitored flight, the aircraft can develop a bank angle and begin a descending turn. The pilot may also inadvertently apply pressure to the flight controls while reaching, introducing roll and pitch inputs they're not aware of. The correct action is to LEAVE THE PEN, maintain aircraft control, and retrieve it only during straight-and-level cruise when the scan can be quickly resumed.

options.label: B
options.text: The pen could jam the rudder pedals, preventing the pilot from controlling the aircraft's yaw axis. The pilot should retrieve it immediately before it causes a flight control restriction.

options.label: C
options.text: The pilot could accidentally disconnect the yoke from the control column while reaching. This is a common mechanical failure mode in GA aircraft.

options.label: D
options.text: The danger is minimal — the aircraft will continue flying straight and level without pilot input for the few seconds needed to retrieve the pen.

questions.explanation: The dropped pen scenario is a classic SA loss trigger. Cognitive tunneling causes the pilot's scan to collapse. The aircraft does NOT fly straight and level without input (Option D) — even a slight trim imbalance or gust creates bank and pitch changes that compound in seconds. The rudder pedal jamming (Option B) is a legitimate concern but secondary to the SA loss from the distraction itself. The correct response is to LEAVE the pen until the flight situation allows safe retrieval.

questions.text: A pilot's VOR receiver shows a red NAV flag over the CDI. The pilot checks: frequency is correct, Morse code identifier is NOT audible, and the circuit breaker is in (not popped). What is the most likely explanation and what should the pilot do?

options.label: A
options.text: The most likely explanation is that the aircraft is too far from the VOR station or terrain is blocking the line-of-sight signal path. VOR operates on VHF frequencies with line-of-sight propagation — mountains, hills, and even the curvature of the Earth can mask the signal. The pilot should: (1) maintain heading and altitude, (2) consider climbing to restore line-of-sight, (3) if climbing doesn't restore the signal, transition to GPS or pilotage as a backup navigation method. If the VOR is within published service volume AND the pilot has clear line-of-sight, then the station may be undergoing maintenance.

options.label: B
options.text: The VOR receiver has failed internally. The pilot should attempt to reset the avionics by cycling the avionics master switch off and back on.

options.label: C
options.text: The NAV flag is a normal indication when the aircraft is close to the VOR station (inside the cone of confusion). The pilot should continue tracking and the signal will return.

options.label: D
options.text: The VOR signal is being jammed by military operations. The pilot should check NOTAMs for VOR interference alerts in the area.

questions.explanation: A NAV flag with correct frequency and NO Morse code identifier most commonly indicates the signal is too weak to receive — either due to distance beyond service volume or terrain masking. The absent identifier confirms the receiver is not receiving a usable signal. If the aircraft is within the published service volume with clear terrain, the station may be in maintenance. Option B is possible but should not be the first assumption — power-cycling avionics risks losing settings. Option C is wrong — the cone of confusion causes needle oscillation but the TO/FROM flag flickers, not a persistent NAV flag. Option D is very unlikely for VOR.

questions.text: During a summer VFR flight, a pilot's iPad is mounted on the glare shield in direct sunlight. After 30 minutes, the iPad displays a temperature warning and shuts down. The pilot has no backup device and no paper charts. What should the pilot do?

options.label: A
options.text: Move the iPad to a shaded location (in the shade of the sun visor or on the side panel) and wait for it to cool. While waiting, maintain the current heading and altitude. Use pilotage (looking outside for landmarks) and dead reckoning (last known position + heading + speed + time) to navigate. If receiving Flight Following, inform ATC of the equipment failure — they can provide radar vectors if needed. When the iPad cools sufficiently (10-15 minutes in shade), restart it and resume normal navigation. Lesson learned: never place the EFB in direct sunlight.

options.label: B
options.text: Declare an emergency — the pilot has lost all navigation capability.

options.label: C
options.text: Land at the nearest airport immediately. Flying without charts is unsafe and potentially illegal.

options.label: D
options.text: Continue to the destination using the aircraft's compass heading. The magnetic compass is always available as a primary navigation tool and charts are not required for VFR.

questions.explanation: An iPad thermal shutdown is an inconvenience, not an emergency (Option B is an overreaction). The pilot can navigate using dead reckoning and pilotage — these are fundamental skills tested on the checkride. ATC can provide radar vectors if needed. The iPad will typically cool in 10-15 minutes in shade. Option C treats the situation as more severe than it is — VFR flight with pilotage is the most basic form of navigation. Option D partially correct about the compass but dismisses the value of charts for position confirmation.

questions.text: A pilot is hand-flying during cruise when they decide to reprogram the GPS to add an intermediate waypoint. The pilot looks down at the GPS display and begins pressing buttons. After 30 seconds of heads-down programming, the pilot glances at the altimeter and notices the aircraft has descended 200 feet and the heading has drifted 15 degrees. What should the pilot's takeaway be?

options.label: A
options.text: The GPS interface is poorly designed and the manufacturer should simplify the programming process.

options.label: B
options.text: The pilot must re-prioritize: AVIATE first, PROGRAM last. GPS programming during flight should be done in small increments — press buttons for 5-10 seconds, then LOOK UP and verify heading, altitude, and airspeed before continuing. The pilot should NEVER spend 30 continuous seconds heads-down. If the programming is complex, engage the autopilot first to maintain attitude while reprogramming. The 200-foot descent and 15-degree drift demonstrate how rapidly an unmonitored aircraft deviates — this is the cognitive tunneling that causes CFIT accidents.

options.label: C
options.text: The aircraft should be able to maintain heading and altitude for 30 seconds without pilot input. The pilot should check the trim settings to ensure the aircraft is properly trimmed for straight-and-level flight.

options.label: D
options.text: 200 feet and 15 degrees is within acceptable tolerances for VFR flight. The pilot should not be overly concerned about minor deviations during routine programming tasks.

questions.sjt_rationale: Option A blames the equipment instead of the pilot's task management. Option C expects perfect stability without input — even well-trimmed aircraft will drift with gusts and slight trim changes. Option D dismisses the deviation as insignificant — 200 feet and 15 degrees in 30 seconds extrapolates to significant deviation over a longer programming session, and is the beginning of the cascade that leads to CFIT. Option B correctly identifies the root cause (heads-down fixation) and prescribes the mitigation (incremental programming with frequent scan recovery).
questions.explanation: GPS programming fixation is one of the most common causes of altitude and heading deviations in modern GA aircraft. The Aviate-Navigate-Communicate-Program hierarchy places programming LAST. If the programming task requires sustained attention, the autopilot should be engaged first to maintain the aircraft state. The 5-10 second 'look down, look up' technique prevents cognitive tunneling.

questions.text: A pilot is navigating a VFR cross-country using GPS as the primary navigation source. The GPS position shows the aircraft over a large lake. The pilot looks out the window and sees farmland with no lake anywhere in sight. What should the pilot conclude?

options.label: A
options.text: The GPS is correct — the lake may be too small to see from altitude, or the pilot may be looking in the wrong direction.

options.label: B
options.text: The GPS position is likely WRONG. When the visual picture out the window contradicts the electronic display, the pilot must not trust the electronics over their own eyes. This could be a spoofing event, a database error, or a RAIM failure. The pilot should: (1) immediately cross-reference with a second independent source — tune a VOR and determine the radial, or use pilotage with the sectional chart to match visual landmarks. (2) If the GPS is confirmed inaccurate, discontinue use and navigate by VOR/pilotage. (3) Inform ATC if receiving services.

options.label: C
options.text: Ignore the discrepancy and continue on the GPS course. Small position errors are common and the GPS will self-correct within a few minutes.

options.label: D
options.text: The sectional chart is probably outdated — the lake may have dried up or been drained since the chart was published.

questions.sjt_rationale: Option A trusts electronics over eyes — the foundational trap that leads to CFIT. If the GPS says you're over water and you see farmland, the GPS is wrong, not your eyes. Option C ignores the discrepancy — 'small position errors' don't put lakes under farmland. Option D fabricates a reason to trust the GPS — a large lake doesn't disappear between chart publications. Option B correctly applies Correlation Navigation: when primary and visual don't match, distrust the primary and verify with an independent source.
questions.explanation: Correlation Navigation means continuously verifying the primary nav system with an independent source — including your own eyes. When the GPS says one thing and the window shows another, the pilot must resolve the discrepancy before continuing. This is the defense against spoofing, database errors, and silent GPS failures. The eyes are always the ultimate authority in VFR flight.
